subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON WELFARE ASSISTANCE AND HOSPITALIZATION FOR IMMIGRANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with your permission I should like to inform hon. members of an announcement which is being made this afternoon jointly by Hon. Louis P. Cecile, minister of public welfare of Ontario, and myself concerning the welfare of immigrants residing in Ontario.
As hon. members know, an agreement was signed in March, 1952 whereby the Ontario department of public welfare and the Department of Citizenship and Immigration shared equally the costs of certain welfare assistance and hospitalization in the case of immigrants who had less than one year's residence in Canada and became indigent through accident or illness.
Hospitalization costs will continue to be shared under the agreement of March, 1952 although in the light of the federally sponsored provincial hospital insurance plan this aspect of the agreement is under discussion with the provincial authorities with a view to possible amendment.
In the case of welfare and in the interests of improved administrative practice, Ontario has agreed as of May 1 to treat immigrants in Canada less than one year the same as other persons in that province under the terms of the Ontario general welfare assistance act, and to share with the federal government such expenses as are applicable under the agreement in force under the federal Unemployment Assistance Act rather than through a separate agreement.
This new arrangement provides that should the need arise an immigrant in Ontario, regardless of length of residence, will be entitled to all the social and welfare benefits available under provincial legislation, including direct relief under the Ontario welfare assistance act, and immigrants will be treated exactly the same as other persons resident
in that province. The proviso that an immigrant must become indigent through accident or illness, which applied in the case of the earlier agreement, has been removed. This in our opinion will greatly assist newcomers who occasionally after their arrival in this country require social and welfare benefits. My department and the national employment service will continue, as in the past, to assist immigrants in their establishment in employment and integration into the Canadian community.
Ontario becomes the first province to accept this responsibility in respect of welfare which affects the majority of immigrants, as something slightly in excess of 50 per cent of the immigrants who come to this country establish themselves in that province. I may add that negotiations have been initiated with some of the other provinces with a view to concluding similar arrangements.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. After lengthy deliberation we have finally come to a ruling. I must tell the committee that it is rather a lengthy document, and I shall appreciate their kindness in listening to it. Yesterday when paragraph 1 of the Excise Tax Act resolution was being considered by the committee, the hon. member for Trinity proposed the following amendment:
That paragraph 1 be stricken out of the resolution and that the following paragraphs be renumbered accordingly.
The Minister of Finance then raised a point of order to the effect that the amendment was out of order in that it was a straight negative. He also suggested that it would be possible

to propose a similar amendment on each subsequent paragraph of the resolution and thereby effect a negative of the whole resolution. Later on in the discussion the minister, in support of his point of order, quoted section 4 of citation 266 of Beauchesne's fourth edition, to the effect that the amendment, if carried, "would alter the balance of ways and means".
With regard to the first point raised by the Minister of Finance, I agree with him that the amendment if carried would be a negative of the proposal contained in paragraph 1 of the resolution. However, in a careful review of the authorities I am unable to find any support for his contention that such an amendment is irregular. In this regard citation 201 of Beauchesne's fourth edition reads as follows:
The object of an amendment may be to effect such an alteration in a question as will obtain the support of those who, without such alteration, must either vote against it or abstain from voting thereon, or to present to the house an alternative proposition either wholly or partially opposed to the original question. This may be effected by moving to omit all the words of the question after the first word, "that", and to substitute in their place other words of a different import. In that case the debate that follows is not restricted to the amendment, but includes the motives of the amendment and of the motion, both matters being under the consideration of the house as alternative propositions.
A motion may be amended: (a) by leaving out certain words; (b) by leaving out certain words in order to insert other words; (c) by inserting or adding other words.
In view of the latter part of the foregoing citation and in the absence of any authority to the contrary, I am inclined to say that the amendment as to form is not irregular.
The second point raised by the minister, namely that the deletion of clause 1 of the resolution is not in order because it alters the balance of ways and means, is one which has been raised time and again during the past 10 or 15 years, and in several cases rulings to that effect have been appealed to the house. The authority for these rulings was initially contained in citation 500 of Beauchesne's third edition, and as a result of the use of this citation a ruling was made in 1951 which now appears as section 4 of citation 266 of Beauchesne's fourth edition. This section reads as follows:
It is not in order to move deletion of a particular clause in an excise tax resolution because it alters the balance of ways and means. Chairman's decision confirmed by the house on a division.
It will be noted that the ruling made by the chairman of the committee of ways and means in 1951 rested entirely on the premise that the amendment would alter the balance of ways and means. In concluding his ruling, 66968-9-211J
Excise Tax Act
as reported on page 2662 of Hansard, May 3, 1951, the then chairman said:
We are agreed all along the line except on that one point. If the hon. member will look at citation 500 of Beauchesne, third edition, he will see why it would be very difficult for the chairman in the Canadian house at least to agree with him that a complicated question can be divided by a member moving that a certain portion of the resolution be deleted. Citation 500 says very clearly that it must not affect the balance of ways and means. Certainly the hon. member will admit that if this amendment should carry, deleting the first paragraph which provides that the rate of the general sales tax shall be increased from eight per cent to ten per cent, the balance of ways and means would be altered. Therefore I would have no alternative but to declare the amendment out of order.
As the meaning of the phrase "must not affect the balance of ways and means for the service of the year" presented something of a mystery, and because the repeated use of it seemed to present an insuperable barrier to the moving of amendments by private members; and moreover, since the phrase was extracted in the first instance from May's thirteenth edition, the Clerk of our house sought the advice of the clerk of the British house in regard to the validity of the principle enunciated in the phrase.
If I may have the indulgence of the committee a little longer I should like to quote several paragraphs from the letter written in reply by the clerk of the British house. This letter is dated January 23, 1959, and I quote from it as follows:
I would like straight away to express my respectful agreement with the ruling of your chairman to the effect that an amendment to reduce a tax is in order.
This paragraph, I should say, refers to a ruling made in 1957. The clerk of the British house continues:
If that were not so, the position would be that the house could reduce a tax to nothing by rejecting the proposal for imposing it but could not moderate the original proposal or ever initiate any moderation once the tax was in existence. That has never been the position at Westminster as is shown by the proceedings in committee on any finance bill.
A committee which is considering a "charge", whether upon the people or upon the revenue, has either to approve, disapprove or reduce that "charge" but may not extend it either in amount or in the area of its operation. (See May 16th edition, pages 772 and 801).
I now turn to the words "must not affect the balance of ways and means for the service of the year". The use made of this quotation seems to me to illustrate the danger of taking words out of their context and I venture to quote the whole passage:
"Proposals for the variation or modification of taxation can therefore be made in the committee: but these proposals must be grafted upon the financial scheme submitted by the government, and must not affect the balance of ways and means voted for the service of the year. Amendments, therefore, can be proposed to substitute another

Excise Tax Act
tax, of equivalent amount, for that proposed by the government, as, for instance, a proposal to substitute probate and legacy duty on real property as an alternative for an inhabited house duty; the necessity of new taxation, to that extent, being already declared on behalf of the crown."
Although I do not propose to quote the passage in full I think a reference to the historical passage on pages 704 and 705 of the 16th edition is necessary fully to comprehend the statement of the present practice which is set out on pages 801 and 802 of the same edition. I think from this it is clear that the passage cited from page 544 of the 13th edition referred to a practice of substituting one charge for another providing the total amount of taxation remained unaltered, and that this practice is now obsolete.
The reference to the thirteenth edition in this paragraph is citation 500 of Beauchesne's third edition. The clerk's letter ends with this paragraph:
In conclusion, to insist that the house can only accept or reject but not modify the financial proposals of the government, which is in fact what the minister was claiming, seems to me a great extension of the financial powers of the crown and to be one which has never been, or is likely to be, accepted by the House of Commons at Westminster.
I regret very much having taken so much of the committee's time with my lengthy statement but in view of the importance of this question I considered it incumbent upon me to deal at length with this problem.
Accordingly, under the circumstances I feel impelled to rule that the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Trinity is in order. Is the committee ready for the question?

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
1. Resolved,
(a)	that it is expedient to amend the english version of the Customs Tariff by adding to section two thereof the following subsection:
(3) The word "machinery" wherever it appears in this Act shall be read and construed as "machines";
(b)	that it is expedient to amend the Customs Tariff by striking out section 13 and substituting the following therefor:
13. (1) The minister may order that, in lieu of the ad valorem rate of duty or the free rate of duty, the specific duty provided for in tariff items 87, 92, 94, 95 and 95a shall apply to goods described in the order imported through ports in a region or part of Canada during such period or periods as may be fixed by the minister.
(2) If before, the coming into operation of an order under subsection (1), a person purchased

goods for importation through a port in a region or part of Canada specified in the order, in the expectation in good faith that the ad valorem rate of duty or the free rate of duty would apply to the goods, and at the time of the coming into operation of the order the goods were in transit to the purchaser in Canada, the ad valorem rate of duty or the free rate of duty shall apply to the goods, notwithstanding the order.

This is an innocent looking resolution, but I think it has implications that are worthy of a fuller explanation than was given by the minister in his budget address. The first part of the resolution concerns the definition of the word "machinery" and "machines". The minister did, of course, refer to this at page 2424 of Hansard for April 9. He summed up his comments by saying:
Thus, there will be no change.
I am not satisfied about this, Mr. Chairman. I should like a more complete explanation from the minister. We have here specifically six types of machines which are to be deemed machines or machinery made in Canada, and the minister has indicated to the house that this involves no change. I should like the minister to give the greatest possible explanation of the reason for this change in definition because I believe at least two of the items to which reference is made, and I think of soft drink and hoist machines, actually were the subject of appeals to the tariff board as to whether or not they were in fact machinery that was made in Canada. I understand the tariff board ruled that they were not. In any event I think paragraph (a), which places a new subsection 3 to section 2 of the Customs Tariff requires more explanation from the minister before we are asked to amend the statute.
Now, if he would like me to deal with this whole resolution, the next amendment is to section 13 of the Customs Tariff. Again I should like a full explanation from the minister as to the reason for this very substantial change in the wording of our statute, and particularly whether or not under the proposed amendments the Minister of National Revenue will have discretion in the matter of imposing higher duties than we would normally contemplate and the number of weeks that will be referred to as the special seasonal period for the various items in the schedule.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If my hon. friend will permit me, Mr. Chairman, may I suggest we deal with the two parts of the resolution separately, that is to say part (a) and part (b). They relate to two different subject matters. I believe you called part (a), Mr. Chairman, and it will contribute to more orderly discussion if we can deal with them separately, if that meets with your approval.
Customs Tariff
Then, Mr. Chairman, if I may take up the point the hon. gentleman was raising with respect to part (a) of the resolution, I would say this concerns a matter of definition, and a matter of definition only. I think the hon. gentleman has confused this matter of definition in resolution 1 (a) with provisions that are to be found in resolution No. 4 at pages 24 and 25 of the printed booklet of ways and means resolutions. We will be coming to those in due course, Mr. Chairman. Those are to be found under item 427 on pages 24 and 25. where certain machines are set out in detail, but the present resolution concerns definition and definition only.
I may say that the problem does not arise in the French version of the Customs Tariff. The English version uses the words "machine" and "machinery" apparently almost indiscriminately, certainly with no clear line of distinction evident. On the other hand the French version uses the one word "machine". What is proposed here is an amendment to the English version of the Customs Tariff Act, and the English version alone.
Lacking any definition or reconciliation in the act of the two words "machine" and "machinery", it seemed to us that it was highly desirable, for the reasons I set forth in the budget speech, that it should be made quite clear in the act what is meant. In ordinary English use the word "machine" suggests at once some individual machine that is capable of some independent operation. The word "machinery" is a broader word. It connotes something in the nature of a mechanical system which might involve the connecting together and operation together of what might otherwise be regarded as a number of individual machines.
Here is the problem, Mr. Chairman. Because this distinction, which I suppose would be apparent to most persons using these words in the English language, does not explain the use of these two words in the customs tariff, we are proposing in this resolution that the word "machinery" is to be given the meaning of "machine" in order that where the word "machinery" is used in the act, it shall be quite clear that it embraces the individual machines which may be part of a mechanical system.
I think the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River will recall that in the budget speech I referred by way of illustration to the machines that are enumerated under item 427 of the tariff, which we will be coming to under resolution No. 4. If it would be of assistance to hon. members I could just make that reference for purposes of illustration, because we will be coming to the changes that are proposed in item 427 when we reach the fourth resolution.

Customs Tariff
There are two items in the tariff under which most imports of machines are classified. Item 427 covers machinery which is ruled by the customs authorities to be "of a class or kind made in Canada" and carries relatively high duties. The other item, 427a, covers machinery which is ruled by customs to be "of a class or kind not made in Canada" and carries relatively low rates of duties. Both these items refer to machinery. Consequently it might be argued that a group of machines whose operation is linked together in one way or another should all be classified under one item or the other as machinery. In this case, if one of the machines in the group was of a class or kind not made in Canada, then the whole group would carry the lower rate of duty notwithstanding the fact that all the other machines in the group were ruled to be made in Canada. This change is proposed in order to make it clear that each machine must be classified on the basis of its particular made in Canada status.

Just having reference to the last few remarks of the minister may I say this. I take it that this question of whether or not a machine would be deemed to be made in Canada and thus be subject, as the minister says, to a higher rate of duty, would have some practical relationship to the size of the machine. In the rewording, is consideration being given to sizing in a realistic way? In other words, when these six particular items are selected as machinery deemed to be made in Canada, it is possible that machinery of a certain size is not made in Canada, but if required by an importer, he would have to pay an extremely heavy rate of duty on it simply because of a change in description in the tariff item and the suggestion that it is now deemed to be made in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No change is proposed in the criteria by which it is established that a machine is or is not of a class or kind made in Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is there any further discussion on resolution 1 (a)? Is there any discussion on resolution 1 (b>?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As to part (b) there is an amendment which I shall ask my colleague the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys to move. It is one which applies strictly to the second resolution relating to fruits and vegetables, but there is an incidental amendment required to resolution

1 (b) in addition to the proposed new wording of section 13 (1) of the act. The amendment simply strikes out of the proposed wording of section 13 (1) the reference to tariff item 95a.
The reason for this is as follows. There will be actually three amendments arising out of this point I am about to mention now.
I gave copies to the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River and the hon. member for As-siniboia. I should say that this is one of three amendments all pertaining to the same matter. It concerns the placing of muskmelons in the same category as cantaloupes in the fruit and vegetable item to which we will be coming under resolution No. 2. This one is simply incidental.
I might say that following the conclusion of negotiations with the United States respecting the proposed changes in the tariff items on fruits and vegetables, the resolution was brought forward in the present form with the understanding that in this form it was fully acceptable to the United States following our negotiations pursuant to the provisions of the general agreement on tariffs and trade. They have drawn to our attention their understanding that muskmelons were to be treated in the same category as cantaloupes for this purpose. We have no serious quarrel with them on this point.
I might explain to the committee what the difference will amount to. In the original budget resolution it was proposed that cantaloupes should be free of duty during the off season and that muskmelons would continue to be dutiable at 10 per cent during the off season. It is now proposed in this series of three amendments to introduce duty free entry in the off season for both cantaloupes and muskmelons by making provision for muskmelons in the same item as cantaloupes. I may say for the assurance of hon. members that the Canadian horticultural council was consulted on this subject and offered no objections.

I do not think the minister has answered the question which I think has greatest relevancy at this stage of the debate. He is proposing to substitute new wording for the existing section 13 of the Customs Tariff. In particular this involves-and this is of great interest to the

public and to the house-ministerial discretion of a very important nature in the matter of setting rates of duty on these articles which go on the tables of our families across the land.

This is rather confusing because there has been an alteration of the points in Nos. 1 and 2. They have been interchanged, and so on. But the minister's discretion under the existing statute, as I understand it, was not to exceed for each regional part of Canada the number of weeks mentioned in the individual items. That to me means that if there were an in season extra duty with respect to some of these vegetables, shall we say for 12 weeks, the minister's discretion was to be limited on each of the vegetable items to that extent. I do not see in the resolution an indication that it is proposed that the minister should be similarly restricted, according to the new phraseology.

Mr. Chairman, as I see it this is the clause we are asked to agree to in principle which will amend the Customs Tariff, as proposed by the minister in the budget address and, as detailed in the many items which are now before us.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether I correctly understand the point raised by the hon. gentleman, but this particular resolution, No. 1 (b), has quite

limited application. It applies simply to section 13 of the act and varies the language of that section having reference to certain changes that follow in the later resolutions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if I may say so I think my hon. friend is quite wrong. The proposed amendments to the Customs Tariff are in different form from the resolutions proposing amendments to the other four statutes with which we have already dealt in the sittings of this committee. In other cases there was simply one resolution with respect to all the amendments to each act. The one resolution was divided into various paragraphs. I think, Mr. Chairman, perhaps the minister misunderstood my intent. I would like to express my appreciation of his outlining to me the various detailed proposals which we will be asked to approve. However, I wish to add a few words as to the overriding question of whether or not it is expedient at this time for the government or

Customs Tariff
the minister to amend the Customs Tariff as a whole. I believe the minister will agree with me that this is the only place at which I can say something which has a general application to the specific matters he is proposing to amend at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I suppose it is well that we should clarify this point now. We have already adopted resolution 1 (a). The hon. member is proceeding now to discuss resolution 1 (b) and he is proposing, as I infer from his remarks, something of a general discussion. I would have thought Mr. Chairman, that the proper place for that was in the budget debate. We are here dealing with a series of specific resolutions proposing specific amendments to the Customs Tariff. I would have thought that discussion of each of these should be relevant to the particular item.

Mr. Chairman, I hope we will not spend any more time on this. However, I was being kind to the minister. I realize at once that resolutions 1 (a) is a matter having to do with terminology and that really the operative clause is 1 (b). The minister, in answer to something which was said by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River a while ago, indicated that he himself regarded 1 (a) as being a matter concerned only with terminology and having very little to do with the overriding principles.
We in this group are not necessarily opposed to each and every one of the amendments which are being offered to the Customs Tariff, but we have a feeling, and we have had it for a number of years, that what the minister is attempting to do, and what he was attempting to do last year, by offering us a multitudinous array of amendments as to detail is attempting to apply axle grease to an intercontinental ballistic missile, and that the amendments in their entirety are completely outmoded in the day and age in which we now live.
We realize that the over-all effect of all these amendments must amount to one thing and one thing only, as was the case a year ago, and that is a higher level of tariffs. I know the minister can haul out all kinds of arguments pointing to where he is in effect reducing tariffs. He did this a year ago. However, in the main a year ago he raised the tariffs and he raised the cost of living to the Canadian consumer. All one need do is look at the expectations, as announced in the budget, and then at the figure actually realized. The minister cannot deny that he is expecting more revenue in the current fiscal year than he obtained in the preceding fiscal year from the changes or amendments in the Customs Tariff which he is proposing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do deny that. As f stated in the budget speech, there is no material effect contemplated in the yield from the Customs Tariff as a result of the proposed changes. I am excepting, of course, those that correspond to the Excise Act changes which were discussed last night.
May I remind the hon. member of the statistics I gave the house in the budget speech as reported in Hansard on page 2422, in the second column, where I said:
It might be of interest to note that 142 tariff items and subitems are affected by the resolutions. In the case of 32 items the rates of duty are being increased. In the case of 40 items the rates are being reduced. In the case of nine items, all involving fruits and vegetables, rates are being both increased and decreased depending on the season. Finally, there are 61 items for which rates of duty are left unchanged and for which the changes proposed are, for the most part, purely formal.
So I think the hon. member will realize that on balance, while one cannot always give changes of this kind equal weight, the result in the total is as much to reduce the tariff as to increase it. And so far as revenue is concerned, apart from those duties affecting spirits which I mentioned last night, we do not, as I indicated in the budget speech, expect any material effect whatever on the revenue from the Customs Tariff as a result of the enactment of the proposed changes.

Well, may I inform the minister that a year ago we were faced with a proposition along very similar lines to the amendments to the Customs Tariff which are proposed this year, and the hon. gentleman on that occasion went to considerable length to impress the committee with the fact that the Customs Tariff was being reduced in more cases than it was being increased. However, I notice from the budget papers, as they are reproduced in Hansard of Thursday, April 9, that whereas the forecast of revenues from customs import duties was $450 million, the revenues actually received amounted to $486 million. In other words the revenues exceeded the minister's announced expectations by the sum of $36 million.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
But that had
nothing to do with the changes in the tariff. We have to make a forecast using the best judgment we can as to what may be the yield from the customs duties having regard to the imports which may be expected. We came reasonably close, but to the extent that the result does not tally precisely with the forecast, that is not attributable to the changes in the tariff but to the over-all effects of imports.

All I can say in reply is that in a year when our imports were well below

expectations we had the minister underestimating the results oi the operation of the Customs Tariff by some 7 per cent. Last year we suffered a decline in imports of a radical nature, yet despite this decline there was this substantial underestimate. If our imports had remained at a normal level, or if they had continued to increase, the minister would have been very much further out in his estimates than he was.
I can understand the minister being out in his estimates to a reasonable extent. However, at a time when imports were declining, and after the minister had left an impression throughout Canada that he had been able to reduce import tariffs more than he had raised them, one would have expected a decline in net revenue under the Customs Tariff rather than receipts $36 million over and above the expectations of the department.
I do not think we can ride several horses at once. This government is either reducing tariffs, or it is leaving them as they are, or it is raising tariffs. There is a feeling abroad now that the Tories have learned nothing since the hungry thirties, and that by one means or another they are continuing to behave as if our economic salvation as Canadians lay in higher tariff rates. The minister may haul out all kinds of details and say, look at the number of items on which I have reduced the tariff. However, if he raises the tariff on a few key commodities he raises the cost of living for all Canadian consumers, and the total effect is a rise in the tariff revenue.
Only a year ago the minister underlined the pressing need to raise the Customs Tariff on British woollens. I was out in rural Ontario over the week end, and I drove past an idle plant in Hespeler. I was told that this plant was at one time the greatest woollen textile factory in the whole British commonwealth of nations. Yet despite the aid which the minister sought to give the industry a year ago by amending the Customs Tariff, that plant has since had to close down. One of our most enterprising industries in that whole area of west central Ontario has had to shut its doors, despite the fact that the minister added to the cost of living of all Canadians who have to buy textiles by the amendments he offered a year ago.
I know the minister realizes that he is somewhat isolated in the world of today in his approach to the Customs Tariff, because hardly anywhere in the whole world, except in the United States and the Dominion of Canada, does one find this age-old approach, this seeking of a solution to our problems based on high tariffs versus low tariffs.

Customs Tariff
Most modern nations of the world today have adopted the policy of assessing their import needs and their export requirements, and for that purpose have established import and export boards. They live in a planned and in a sensible way, instead of continuing this nonsensical farce of attempting to make some people in Canada believe that we are a high tariff people, and making other people in Canada believe we are opposed to high tariffs. The net result of this ridiculous economic nationalism that we have been sowing the seeds of for a number of years now in Canada has always in all history resulted in unemployment, misery, poverty, want and, in many instances, world war.
If the minister, rather than making these proposed amendments, were to offer an overall amendment whereby we might ally ourselves with the European economic union now being formed, he would be breaking new ground, he would be making a real contribution to the restoration of Canadian prosperity. With respect to the (b) paragraph of this resolution, I can understand that. The minister has cleared up one point that I had raised when I compared the new phraseology with the old. I am not proposing to debate the merits of this at this time since we shall have an opportunity to do that on the presentation of the bill, but I realize that

Customs Tariff
there has been a change in the key tariff item numbers which necessitated the amendment of this particular section of the existing act. I should like to hear from the minister a little better explanation of why he has completely revamped the language of the section and has gone far beyond just simply substituting for the old tariff item numbers the new ones that result from the tariff board report and the resolutions which are to follow.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the proposed new language is a drafting improvement on the language of the existing section 13; it is very much clearer. It does not change the essence of the old provisions at all as applied to ministerial discretion, which is the point the hon. member raised earlier.
It is in this section 13 of the Customs Act that we find provided the authority for the regional application of the seasonal duties on fruits and vegetables. As hon. members are aware, many of those products are first available from domestic production on the west coast. Then, somewhat later they are available in Ontario, Quebec, the maritimes or the Atlantic areas. In certain instances they are produced in only one region of Canada; for example, apricots in British Columbia. Of course, in some areas, owing to poor growing conditions, there will be a short crop in a particular region. result in any net gain in revenue and are more of a protective nature than anything else. He confirmed this point when he said, as found on page 2423 of Hansard of April 9:
Turning to the canned and frozen products there are modest increases of duty consequential upon the increased protection received by the fresh products.
A few minutes ago the minister referred to three separate regions of Canada, the west coast, central Canada and the maritime provinces. In the province from which I come conditions are such that we should be considered as a separate region. Conditions there are totally different from those that obtain anywhere on the mainland. I realize how difficult it is for the government to lay down one single rule that will bear evenly on all sections of a large country like Canada. While it is difficult to see how anyone is going to benefit from this extra protection, certainly no consumer anywhere in Canada will benefit and in the case of my province it is going to constitute a real hardship.
In Newfoundland we already have the highest cost of living in all Canada and the effect of these tariff changes will be to push it higher still. One of our main complaints as a province since confederating with Canada has been and still is that we are a captive market forced to buy on the mainland and particularly in the central provinces. This, however, does not hold true in the case of fresh fruits and vegetables. As far as Newfoundland is concerned, this protection will not benefit mainland producers at all because we are not able to buy in that market in any case. The reasons for that are obvious. In the first place, our population is scattered around a 6,000-mile coastline and is broken up into about 1,300 isolated settlements. There are no refrigeration facilities for storage of fresh fruits and vegetables, and there is a lack of transportation facilities as well.
We are handicapped also by the fact that we have a narrow gauge railway which prevents our importers from buying in carload lots. A fruit vendor in Halifax can buy a carload of fruit originating in California or Florida and have it delivered to his door in Halifax. This is impossible for the Newfoundland merchant because our narrow gauge railway prevents it. Instead, we are forced to buy from brokers in Montreal and this, in itself, makes the cost of fruits and vegetables much higher than in the maritime provinces. In addition to that, we have to go to the extra expense of packaging the goods and pay for the extra handling involved in unloading the foods from trains to the boat, then unloading them from the boat

into railway cars again for transportation to the centres of distribution and from there to the smaller settlements.
This extra packaging must be of the same quality as that required for export, which is much more expensive than the packaging required for the domestic market on the mainland. If all that were not enough, we find that the Maritime Freight Rates Act apparently does not apply to fruits imported into Canada through maritime ports. I have just had a case brought to my attention where a buyer in Newfoundland bought a carload of fruit in South Africa and had it routed through Saint John, New Brunswick. He then found that instead of the special maritime freight rates applying from Saint John, New Brunswick to Newfoundland, he had to pay an extra 20 per cent freight charge and another i\ per cent terminal charge. We are greatly handicapped, therefore, with respect to fresh fruits and vegetables. Even in St. John's and the large urban centres of our province, fruits and vegetables are at least double the cost in the maritime provinces and are sometimes three or four times as expensive as they are in central Canada.
Now, for these reasons, our Newfoundland people have to rely to a large extent on canned products, particularly canned fruits and vegetables. We have been told that fruits are essential to health. They are a source of minerals and vitamins necessary for the maintenance of health, particularly for the health of children. The only way in which we can maintain a balanced diet in that respect is by the use of canned products. We all know that tariff changes result in price increases that are much greater than the amount of the tariff itself. We have had proof of that recently when a two cent increase in the tax on a package of cigarettes resulted in a four cent increase in the retail price. The result of this tariff change on tinned fruits in particular, plus the other taxes applicable, will prevent our Newfoundland fishermen from obtaining these essential foods at all because they will be priced right out of his pocket.
Apart from that, we have heard a lot from the present government about their intention of encouraging commonwealth trade. Since a great deal of our imported fruit in Newfoundland comes from New Zealand, South Africa and other commonwealth countries, these tariff increases seem to be a peculiar way of achieving that objective. In view of the problems which I have outlined to the minister, I would be most grateful if he would look into the matter to see if it would be possible to create a fourth region which would at least take into account the particular conditions which obtain in my province. I have

particular reference to the way in which the fishermen and poorer people living in the isolated settlements of my province may be affected.

Mr. Chairman, the members of parliament from the Niagara district have always been greatly interested in the tariff on fruits and vegetables. I was reading the debates in May, 1926, in which the Hon. J. D. Chaplin, who was then the member for Lincoln, was talking about the difficulty the producers had in disposing of their fruits and vegetables at favourable prices when fruit from the United States was coming in and was very competitive. He was the minister of trade and commerce in the Meighen administration. During that time, and afterwards, there were only minor changes in the tariff.
In May, 1930 Hon. Charles Dunning brought in a budget and made a real attempt at that time to apply a specific duty over specific periods of time that would correspond to the harvest time of different fruits and vegetables. In presenting his budget at that time he said, and I will paraphrase it, that a combination of specific and ad valorem duties would meet the urgent needs of the growers, acute instability of prices, and at the same time guarantee to consumers at all seasons of the year supplies of these products at reasonable prices. The specific seasonal duties were applied to practically all fruits and vegetables grown in Canada and the application of them has been continued up to the present time.
I have often said in this house that these particular periods for the application of specific duties do not correspond to the harvesting periods of the different fruits and vegetables. One of the reasons for this is that producers have developed different varieties of fruits and vegetables that ripen over a longer time. Another reason is the modern development of cold storage facilities. In other words, importers are able to bring in fruits and vegetables from the United States ahead of the time for the application of the specific duty, those fruits and vegetables could be placed in Canadian cold storage and would be very competitive with our fruits and vegetables when they come on the market. Then, too, at the end of the season the United States producers are able to keep their fruits and vegetables in cold storage in the United States, then bring them in to Canada in competition with our fruits and vegetables at that particular time at the end of our season.

AMENDMENT RESPECTING RIGHT OF APPEAL OF DEPORTATION ORDER
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-20, to amend the Immigration Act (jurisdiction of courts).
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is a measure which I feel should have the unanimous approval of every member in the house who is concerned with the right of people to have appropriate recourse when they feel themselves aggrieved. I think this is a principle which has long been approved and supported in our system of government and in our system of justice. I find that section 39 of the Immigration Act denies that full right, that full freedom, for people who feel themselves aggrieved and wish to seek redress. In order to follow the argument logically I should like to invite hon. members to look at section 39. Let me read it:
No court and no judge or officer thereof has jurisdiction to review, quash, reverse, restrain or otherwise interfere with any proceeding, decision or order of the minister, deputy minister, director, immigration appeal board, special inquiry officer or immigration officer had, made or given under the authority and in accordance with the provisions of this act relating to the detention or deportation of any person, upon any ground whatsoever, unless such person is a Canadian citizen or has Canadian domicile.
The wording of the section is certainly all-inclusive and aims, as the wording clearly indicates, to prevent any court, any judge or officer thereof from dealing with any decision made in connection with a deportation, as set forth in this section; not only does this concern a decision of the minister but also a decision of the deputy minister, a director or immigration officer, meaning almost any immigration official, whether he is in the upper echelons of the department or not, who deals with a matter of this kind.

He makes the decision and the person aggrieved has absolutely no recourse. He must accept it as though it were the decision of the highest court in the land. I feel, Mr. Speaker, that a section in an act which is so restrictive as to prevent a person from seeking redress is not a section which should form part of the law of this country.
Hon. members may be surprised to know that I was a member of the committee in 1953 which adopted this section of the act. Of course, one could properly say, "did you speak up at that time in protest against the inclusion of this section"? I want to draw to hon. member's attention the fact that I did, and I now quote from the minutes of the committee meetings when they considered Bill No. 305 respecting immigration in 1952 and 1953. I shall now quote from page 75:
Section 39: Jurisdiction of courts.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING RIGHT OF APPEAL OF DEPORTATION ORDER
speechtext: I suggest that section 39 merits a little attention. I think that the minister, like human beings, or departmental officials, or boards of inquiry, is human and is prone to misjudge a situation. I do not think they should assume the responsibility, and it is a difficult responsibility of rendering a final judgment which is almost equivalent to the highest court in the land. I think we should allow the man who feels aggrieved by the decision which the minister or the department or the board of inquiry might make, to be permitted to have his day in court; and I think we should work out some machinery to allow a person ordered deported to address himself to the courts.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING RIGHT OF APPEAL OF DEPORTATION ORDER
speechtext: Judges are human!

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING RIGHT OF APPEAL OF DEPORTATION ORDER
speechtext:
That is true, but they are not interested persons; they are not accusers, prosecutors, and judges at the same time. While the department in the very best of faith unfortunately can be in that position, the courts are not.
Lower down the minister made this observation:
As 1 understand Mr. Crestohl he believes that the evidence taken by an inquiry should form the basis of a court proceeding which would pass through the hands of the minister and go to a judge of some kind in a provincial court. I am free to confess that such a proceeding would probably relieve the department of some work and would relieve the minister of exercising his discretion; but if adopted it would introduce entirely new procedures into the immigration proceedings.
Hon. members will see that in 1952, when the government of which I was a follower and supporter dealt with this legislation, I opposed it then. I merely point this out to prove that I am consistent in my opposition. At that time the minister stated that what this would do would be to alter the proceedings in the department of immigration and introduce new procedures. On the question of modifying existing regulations or changing the act, I say respectfully that if the reasons advanced then are the only ones why justice should not be preserved for an aggrieved person, they are not sufficient. One is entitled to have a grievance heard by a tribunal so that he may obtain justice.

In the debate a few minutes ago the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) pointed out that so far as tariff matters are concerned a person who feels himself aggrieved because of a tariff decision has a right of appeal first to the minister; if he is still unhappy about the decision he also has a right of appeal to the tariff board; he then has a right of appeal to the Exchequer Court of Canada, and finally he has a right of appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada. This was clearly explained by the Minister of Finance a few minutes ago. One is really shocked and appalled to find that when dealing with matters of dollars and cents, with tariff questions, there are four stages of appeal in order to seek redress and justice but under the Immigration Act, which deals with human liberty and human rights, there is no right of appeal. It is really incongruous.
An immigration official in the very best of faith talks to an immigant and makes a decision. "I, immigration official, decide that you are to be deported." That decision is as formidable as a judgment of the Supreme Court of Canada. I respectfully submit that such a situation is inconsistent with the reasoning of every member of the house and inconsistent with our basis of justice.
On very many occasions the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) has condemned the arbitrary decisions that the immigration department has been able to make and he promised that if he were given the opportunity he would alter the situation. I should like to quote a statement he made as found in the Toronto Star of April 26, 1957. Among other things he said that he would-
-end the "bureaucratic" interpretations of the Immigration Act and ensure that humanitarianism would be considered more often in handling immigration applications.
What could be more humane, what could fall more within the scope of the Prime Minister's statement than to say to a person who has been told by an immigration official that he is to be deported that he has a right of appeal. The official may have made a mistake in the very best of faith but unfortunately once he has made his decision the door is closed and the person is deported. In all justice and to be consistent with the Prime Minister's statement that humanitarianism will be applied in dealing with immigration regulations, I respectfully submit that the proposed amendment to modify section 39 in order to grant the right of appeal under certain conditions should be adopted. We do not want frivolous appeals, we do not want appeals for the purpose of delay, but if a person is serious enough to make a deposit as security for costs, as I have suggested in the amendment, and if he complies
Immigration Act
with the other conditions he certainly should be entitled to have his day in court. I should also like to quote another statement of the Prime Minister found in the Globe and Mail of April 27, 1957, which report reads as follows:
The Conservatives, he continued, will end the arbitrary and unjust interpretation of immigration regulations which . . . have constituted a denial and veto of immigration legislation.
These two statements of the Prime Minister were both very lofty in principle and in their sense of justice, and I know that he was serious when he made them. I am prepared to accept them and certainly the country will accept them. One way of giving some meaning to the statements of the Prime Minister is to remedy what I and many others consider to be an evil in the present regulations. To deny a human being justice if a minor immigration official should make a mistake by not permitting a right of appeal certainly is beyond every concept of justice as we understand it in Canada.
I have therefore introduced the bill now before us. I had hoped that the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mrs. Fair-clough) would have taken up the bill. I am prepared to withdraw my bill if she will make a statement to the house that section 39 will be remedied. I am not particularly concerned whether it becomes law through a measure presented by me or one presented by the minister as long as it becomes law and human beings are permitted to have their day in court when they are aggrieved so that they may be able to receive justice. I do not want to delay the house in discussing this matter. One could certainly enter into a long debate on the principles of justice but I think that would be elementary and unnecessary. I have presented the situation as I see it and I respectfully submit to the house that the bill should be favourably considered.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING RIGHT OF APPEAL OF DEPORTATION ORDER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill No. C-20 purports to make drastic changes in the Immigration Act. I have heard the hon. member who has just taken his seat trot out the horrors. He referred to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and his pending bill of rights and suggested that we are neglecting the rights of those who intend to become citizens.
Apparently the criticism of the present section of the act is that these persons are not allowed their day in court. However, if one reads the whole act one comes to section 31, and I would direct the attention of all hon. members to that section which sets out in some detail in four subsections the rights of appeal. It is true that if you read section

Immigration Act
39 as it now stands carelessly you might be led to believe that there is no appeal.
But section 31 of the act, and similar provisions, have been used in hundreds of cases before the courts of Canada. I might say that at present there are six rather important cases before the courts. I am, naturally, not able to name them because they are still before the courts. But if you go to the Canadian abridgement you will see dozens and dozens of cases listed in which appeals have been made from decisions of minor officials and of the minister himself.
The suggested amendment in Bill No. C-20, far from enlarging the rights of applicants for citizenship, brings in one or two restrictions. If you go to appeal under this Immigration Act now there is no necessity for putting up a bond, certainly in the first stage of the appeal. If a man got off a ship and an order was made for his deportation, the machinery for appeal is plainly here for all to see. If hon. members are trotting out the horrors, as I said, and trying to pretend that these persons are not getting their rights before the courts of Canada, then I say that is just not true.
There is another amendment which I noticed in this bill which suggests that 30 days of grace be allowed in which to launch this appeal. There is no time limit, Mr. Speaker, under the present administration of this act so I feel if you insert a 30-day period of grace you are not going to assist these people who are allegedly being neglected by our Canadian laws.
I return again to the monetary angle. It would seem to me that if we asked a penniless stowaway to put up $300 before he can have his case heard we would be imposing a serious restriction on his rights.
The amendment also suggests that there would be some difficulty concerning domicile, and I think again this is the result of a careless reading of section 39. A great many of the hundreds of cases reported refer to persons who are neither Canadian citizens nor do they pretend to be. The rights which we extend to these persons are the same rights which we give to Canadian citizens. Although section 39 as it now stands reads awkwardly, if any criticism should be directed toward this section I think it should be directed toward the administration of it. Let us suppose that the minister, having reviewed a case brought to her under section 31, makes what the aggrieved person feels to be an injudicious decision. This person still has recourse to all the historical writs.
I refer again to the reported cases. They are so numerous that I will not bore the house by listing them, but if you look at these cases you will see that they have been

instituted, in the final analysis, by writs. These are writs of certiorari, prohibition and habeas corpus. They all have the same effect, and that is bringing in the back door something which cannot be brought in the front door. Even when a man is under detention awaiting deportation, a writ of habeas corpus might still be issued and he would be brought before the court. I fail to see, Mr. Speaker, how the rights of these persons are in any way withheld under the present act. I can only say that the amendments suggested by Bill No. C-20 would restrict those rights to an even greater degree.
In the last sentence of section 39 of the act we find the phrase, "unless such person is a Canadian citizen or has Canadian domicile". I agree that that is a suggestion that the act does not cover these cases but I say again that the act, as it is administered, gives these applicants the full protection of British law.

Let us consider these

particular points. If we refer to section 5, the medical section, in subsections (a), (b) and (s), there is no right of appeal on a refusal of admittance under a medical certificate. Nor is there under section 19 subclause (1), paragraph (d), which deals with convictions under the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act. There is absolutely no right of appeal. I might cite again section 7, subsection (5), of the present act. You would have to amend the act. As a matter of fact, if we amended section 39 as requested by the hon. member, we would have to go and amend section 7, subsection (5), because you would have a clear inconsistency. May I cite section 7, subsection (5):
(5) The minister may make a deportation order against a person referred to in subsection (4) and such person has no right of appeal from the deportation order and shall be deported as soon as practicable.
If you amend it in one place, I submit you must amend it in another. With all due respect, I would rather think that the point which the hon. member is getting at is this subsection here and not section 39 because I would submit that section 39 allows a certain class of people to have recourse to the courts.
A few moments ago I mentioned section 14 of the Citizenship Act. We have gone a stage further. As to a person who is otherwise qualified as a landed immigrant in this country and applies for citizenship, the court in its examination of the applicant may agree but the minister has the full right to refuse and the applicant has no appeal. Let us say, for the sake or argument, that there should be a right of appeal. I would place these people in the same category as the ones about which the hon. member speaks. We may speak of an absolute right to be heard. But I would ask the hon. gentleman whether there are any such things today as absolute rights. I do not believe there are such things for the individual. In today's international relations and in our relationships one with another there comes a time when perhaps the common good may override the right of the individual. We certainly see it in wartime.
Let us consider but one aspect. I do not say that this is the sole aspect that determines the matter or serves as the basis for this section and section 14 in the Citizenship Act. And, my hon. friend would fully recognize the impossible position in which we would be put. I am speaking here of where there are certain fields where the common good must override any suggestion of an absolute right of the individual. For purposes of security I do not have to dot the "i's" and cross the "t's" for the hon. member to indicate precisely what would happen if a potential deportee

had an order against him because of his background and connections, which posed in the eyes of the laws of this country a threat to the security of the country. He can come forward in court and say, "Prove your case against me." It is a most difficult question and I do not think that the hon. member or I can come down with a 100 per cent answer.
As I indicated initially, I too was bothered as a lawyer about this denial of the right of appeal, and I will say that perhaps I can go a long way towards the point of view expressed by the hon. member. But I am just wondering how far we can go. After all, as the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Bigg) indicated, there are a number of cases presently before the courts where the applicant, the deportee, does not allege that he is a Canadian citizen or that he has acquired domicile. But he is being heard in court. I do not think we can go quite as far as the hon. member would like. In any event, Mr. Speaker, I think I have indicated that he is perhaps applying a patch in a very doubtful area. I think he would find himself in almost as difficult a spot under section 7, subsection
5.	At best you would have a blatant inconsistency in the act. At the moment it is not there. Bearing in mind that the hon. minister has indicated that immigration policy would be subject to review, I do not honestly think that now would be the time to apply what I consider a somewhat dubious patch to this act.

Because the kind of things which used to be said on this side of the house when I was administering the Immigration Act are very much out of accord with the very moderate and judicial statements they have made.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING RIGHT OF APPEAL OF DEPORTATION ORDER
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has just argued his case, so perhaps he will let me now argue mine. I was accused of denying people the right of access to the courts, which I never did at any time. I was accused by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) of all sorts of arbitrary activity, of which the hon. member for Cartier has given a couple of examples. I will not repeat them by

putting them on the record, but I must say that after administering the Immigration Act from July 1, 1954 until June 21, 1957, a period of almost three years, I came to a conclusion which leads me to support the bill moved by the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl) today.
I would like to tell hon. members why I reached that conclusion. I think the hon. member for Athabasca is largely right in what he said, that any person with an ingenious enough lawyer and a sympathetic judge can get his case before the court, and in some provinces this is much easier than in others. There are other provinces where because there is a stricter interpretation of the act it is not so easy. I will not reflect in any way on the bar in any province, but I know there were gross discrepancies. My experience was that all the most dubious cases and all the cases which I thought deserved the least consideration always got into the courts, and a great many cases where the persons were not so persistent or ingenious, or perhaps not so anxious to beat the laws of Canada, never did get to the courts.
As hon. members who interested themselves in this subject know, I did take the responsibility of recommending to my colleagues the setting up of an appeal board against deportation orders made against landed immigrants. That appeal board went as far as the Immigration Act itself allowed, because the Immigration Act says the appeal in the ultimate resort is to the minister. I gave every applicant a choice between appealing to the minister or appealing to the board, and I said that if they chose to appeal to the board and indicated that in their appeal I would not interfere with the judgment of the board. If on the other hand they preferred to appeal to the minister, I would then seek the advice of the board but would have to take my responsibility under the act and make the final decision. From the day that board was set up until I ceased to be minister, and as far as I know I have never heard of any difficulties since although perhaps the hon. lady may know of some, I do not think there has been any trouble about appeals from landed immigrants. I have never heard of any case where it was alleged there was any injustice.
These difficulties all arise in the case of persons who are visitors to Canada, either voluntary visitors or, in some cases as far as the country is concerned, involuntary visitors. No doubt the hon. lady remembers one celebrated case, as would the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Taylor) if he were here. These people are not citizens or
Immigration Act
landed immigrants and have, strictly speaking, no rights except human rights. I came to the conclusion-and this is the reason I am standing here and saying I have completely changed my mind about this-that it would be preferable, and certainly preferable for the minister involved as well as for the reputation of the country, that instead of having to use a backdoor method which has to be used now in many of these cases we could provide in the law for a regular procedure whereby these cases could be taken directly into the courts under appropriate circumstances.
I think the hon. member for Edmonton West has pointed to a difficulty in respect of section 7. Section 7 is very rarely used and there is some question about whether it really serves very much purpose in the act at all. But I think the hon. member is probably right in saying that if section 7 were left as it is and the bill proposed by the hon. member for Cartier were adopted there would be an inconsistency in the act. That is the kind of inconsistency which could easily be fixed up in committee and I do not think it would constitute an insuperable difficulty, or indeed any real difficulty at all to the enactment of this legislation if parliament were so minded.
There is something, too, in what the hon. member for Edmonton West has said about the fact that the hon. lady has promised us in the near future a revision, I took it not merely of the regulations, but also of the act itself.
My hon. friend from Cartier has indicated that if the hon. lady were to say she was considering favourably this proposal of his for inclusion in her general amendments, he would be glad to drop his bill, since he would feel it had served its purpose. I do think the principle of this bill is, on the whole, a sound one. That does not mean that every appeal is going to be successful. I would, in fact, expect that so long as the general ideas prevail which seemed to have prevailed in this country over the years, and which have been reflected in the Immigration Act over the years, most of these appeals would not be successful.
However, there is no doubt that this procedure would remove from the minds of many people the feeling that the administrative officers or the minister were acting both as judge and as an interested party in these cases. While this was not a proper statement of the facts, if it is widely believed to be a proper statement of the facts and if it creates in people's minds a sense of injustice, I can see a very great advantage in the course suggested, a course which would enable these misgivings to be

Immigration Act
removed by legislation which would enable people to go to the courts and have their cases considered by a tribunal which is independent and which obviously has no axe to grind.
I am not at all impressed by the observations of the hon. member for Edmonton West about the Citizenship Act. It is a separate act of parliament. It stands on its own feet, and whether or not it should be amended is an entirely separate question. There is no reason whatever why we should not fill in a pothole on Wellington street just because there is one on Sparks street, and there is no reason why we should not amend the Immigration Act just because the Citizenship Act may require amendment. The hon. member guessed, if he did not know, why that provision was in the Citizenship Act. It was put in there on security grounds. Having administered that act for some time, I am not sure that it is not a rather blunt instrument. I hope that next session when the hon. lady sets up this committee on the Citizenship Act which she promised, this matter will be looked into.

Mr. Speaker, I fear I shall not have time to complete the remarks I had intended to make, but I will begin, and attempt to make my position clear.
At the outset, I should like to say that as a matter of principle I am in favour of

the right to appeal from the decision of an administrative board or tribunal wherever that course is humanly possible. In my opinion a bureaucratic decision or a decision made by a department has elements in it which are unfavourable. I think that in principle we should not tend to move toward making decisions by a government department final, and to that extent I agree with the principle of this bill.
Having said that, however, I should like to look at the measure more closely and point out what I believe to be its shortcomings. I had some other remarks to make, but having regard to the time available I will come immediately to my main point. There are always a number of cases where the security of the country is involved. I feel that to the very point where this is so, the right of appeal should be given. However, the hon. member's bill does seem to have this shortcoming-that no exception is made to cover such circumstances. I believe that had the bill stated that a right of appeal would be granted in any case except where the minister declared that the national interest must override the right of appeal, one of the major objections to his measure would have been removed. But there is no exception made in terms of this bill.
It is very difficult to decide at exactly what point the basic right of an individual to appeal to the courts and have his case heard in public ends, and where the national interest begins. However, it has been the practice for many years in this country that a statement by a minister who has the facts before him that the national interest would not be served by a certain case coming into open court has been accepted. We know many cases where the courts in Canada have gone a long way in this respect. We know of cases where mounted policemen who have been engaged in investigation work-men who have, perhaps, completed many years of investigation into certain cases-have been obliged to come before the courts in order to give their evidence, and immediately, at that point, having been identified, their usefulness as investigators and agents has ceased. That, to my mind, is an indication of the length to which we should go in protecting the rights of the people to appeal to the courts and to have their cases heard.

Customs Tariff
that is required by any paper-making company, and may not be of the speed that is required by any paper-making company.
Item 427 (6) refers to parts thereof. What would happen in the case of a paper-making company that had imported a paper-making machine four, five or ten years ago, and now has to import parts for that machine which are not made in Canada? I do not understand the reasoning behind saying that these parts should be deemed as a class or kind made in Canada. This seems to me to be an increase in the rate of tariff on equipment used in the paper-making industry at a time when even though the paper-making industry forms a very important segment of the economy of this country, yet I think we are entering into a period when we can see that in the years that lie ahead-I do not think it is going to happen tomorrow-the Canadian paper-making industry is going to face keener competition than it has ever known before.
For example, in 1957 the Canadian production of newsprint was something over 6 million tons, 43 per cent of the total world production. Canada used only 3.3 per cent of the world production. Over 5 million tons were shipped to the United States. On the other hand, the United States produced something over 2 million tons, only 14 per cent of the total world production, and yet they used 48.8 per cent of the total world production. Now, it seems to me it would be economically sound if the United States were to begin to produce to fill some of this great demand for paper which they have. Of course, if they had the raw materials to produce that paper it would be a sound business venture. Not too long ago we can remember that in order to make newsprint the best of black spruce was required, and in every batch of pulp a large percentage was black spruce. Then, only a few years ago we got to the point where a fairly large percentage of balsam fir could be used. We now have the situation that in the southern states newsprint is being made from southern pine. We have the same sort of situation in France, and having in mind the progress that is being made in the chemistry of papermaking I think we can feel sure that within a few years paper will be made not only from southern pine in the southern states but also from hardwoods.
Russia is not included in the ten great newsprint producing countries of the world but I believe that within the next few years we will find that Russia will not only invade the papermaking industry but will also invade the paper markets. Therefore it is my opinion that within the not too distant future Canada is going to face very keen competition in the paper industry, and it is for that reason that

I believe that any tendency to increase the tariff on machines being brought in by the paper industry is most inopportune at this time.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OP REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not intend at this time to go into detail on the contents of the bill which will follow this resolution. I shall do that on second reading and when

the bill is before the house. At this stage, Mr. Chairman, 1 shall confine myself to outlining in a general way the provisions which will be forthcoming in the bill.
In brief, the resolution proposes to increase contributions to the unemployment insurance fund by government, by management and by those who will be benefiting under the act. The reason for this is to maintain the fund in a situation of stability over the next few years. During the past two years of recession which we have experienced there has been a pretty heavy drain on this fund. In my opinion it is not anticipated that such a drain will occur again next year. Nevertheless I feel it is good business to place the fund on a sound actuarial basis. It is also my opinion that the government's responsibility is such that it should see that the fund will be able to meet whatever eventualities may arise. At the same time I would like to make it clear, Mr. Chairman, that it is not the government's intention to adopt an inflexible attitude in this regard. I hope the situation will be reviewed from time to time in the light of the requirements of the fund, and should it be possible, as an example, a year from now to look at the situation and find it is possible to reduce the rates, then most certainly that action would be taken.
In these amendments we are establishing two new classes; that is, one class of $33 per week and one of $36. We are also raising the ceiling from $4,800 to $5,460. The purpose of that is to bring back under the act those who were included originally. They were a foreman or his equivalent, but because of the rise in wages over the period of time some 80,000 have been excluded from the act. It is our intention, by raising the ceiling to $5,460, to bring back those 80,000 as contributors to the fund who would enjoy the coverage of the act. Allowable earnings are being increased to the extent of 50 per cent of the benefits. We are also taking care of prison inmates. That is something the hon. member for Vancouver East has propagated, as also have other societies in Canada who are interested in the rehabilitation of prisoners after they have served their term.
In general the purpose of the amendment is to give stability to the fund, to extend coverage to a number of persons who do not now have it, and also to increase the benefit period from 36 weeks to 52 weeks, which brings it back to the status which was in existence prior to the amendments of 1955. This last provision, I might say, has been one which has been requested by a great many organizations, and is one of the promises made by this government during the last two campaigns. There are other amendments to 66968-9-2134
Unemployment Insurance Act correct existing anomalies of minor nature under the act at the present time.
After the second reading it is my wish to refer these amendments to the standing committee on industrial relations so that the members of that committee may go into detail on all of these amendments now proposed to the Unemployment Insurance Act.
