speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure we have all listened with interest to what the Minister of Labour has had to say in his brief statement on this important resolution, a resolution which my hon. friend will remember we urged early in the session should be brought forward at the earliest possible moment. We did so because, in the face of the serious unemployment problem, it was wondered whether or not this measure would provide any kind of relief, by way of maintenance, to many out of work. But it is clear from the account given by the minister a few moments ago that, meritorious as these amendments may be, generally they are not calculated to contribute in any way to the problem of unemployment that now prevails.
As I listened to the minister and as I read the resolution, I assume that the main purpose of the bill which will be founded on this resolution is to raise the rate of remuneration of insurable employment, to increase the rates of contributions to be paid on behalf of insured persons and employers, to add new grounds for extensions of the qualifying periods, to provide a new schedule of rates of benefits consequential on the new table of contributions, and to provide the maximum benefits under the heading "Duration of Benefit", which I imagine will be increased. All we can assume is that the stories which have appeared in the newspapers give correct indications of what is to occur. Then it is proposed to establish a new schedule of allowable earnings and to provide for other related matters.
The minister was frank in saying that one of the reasons for the introduction of this measure was to maintain the integrity of the fund, a fund which has been very seriously invaded during the past 18 months; so seriously, in fact, that if we have a level of unemployment next fall and next winter comparable to the level last winter and last fall there might not be enough money in the fund to take care of the needs contracted for by employers and employees, together with the more modest contribution made by the government of Canada.
As I said, the minister mentioned that one of the purposes of this bill was to guarantee the integrity of the fund, and in this connection it is interesting to recall his own

Unemployment Insurance Act words which will be found in Hansard for 1955 at page 4760 when he said, among other things:
If we look at the fund from 1942 to 1955 we find that at no time was it seriously impaired. We see that it has increased gradually at the rate of about $70 million a year, with one exception when in one year it increased only to the extent of $30 million. To my mind, therefore, there is no danger of serious impairment of the fund, even if the maximum period of 51 weeks were placed in the act.
So in 1955 when the hon. gentleman was on this side of the house he was not concerned about the integrity of the fund. Indeed, he had no reason to be. That is not the situation today, as he himself has acknowledged. The minister was confirmed in the confidence he showed in the past, by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration who, also in 1955, as reported in Hansard at pages 4626 and 4627 said:
I am not worried about the condition of the fund. Not a bit. It is my opinion that after these new provisions have been in effect for a year the fund will be even healthier than it is today. I base that opinion on the fact that from the actuary's own calculations there is every expectation of a net profit.
Later on in my remarks I propose to deal with the figures which indicate what the situation was then, and what the situation is now. I simply wanted to deal with this aspect of the question in a general way at the outset, because the minister himself said that one of the reasons for bringing forward this resolution was to see that the integrity of the fund was maintained. I think we ought to begin by putting first things first.
This particular amendment, like other amendments brought in by the administration in the course of the last year and a half, is an amendment which is being proposed with respect to an act brought in by a Liberal administration, an act which in this period of heavy unemployment has served the people of Canada, and particularly the unemployed, in a most gratifying manner. When we think of the serious problems and vicissitudes which have affected the unemployed population of Canada, for the last year and a half in particular, we can all be grateful that we had an Unemployment Insurance Act in being and that there was available for its operation a large fund to which contributions had been made by three bodies and, particularly, by two-the workers and management-thereby bringing to the unemployed, as a matter of right, assistance which in this period of unemployment was so essential to them.

But before dealing with the merits of the resolution I think there is one piece of unfinished business to be done, and that concerns a matter which was referred to yesterday in answer to questions put by the hon. member for Assiniboia and by the Leader of the Opposition. One of the posts on the unemployment insurance commission had become vacant. Mr. R. J. Tallon, the former secretary treasurer of the trades and labour congress, has resigned, or his term of office has come to an end. I think I am expressing the views of every member of this house and, certainly, the views of all of those who have had anything to do with this matter, when I say that Mr. Tallon has earned our warmest gratitude for his services as the labour representative on the unemployment insurance commission for a long period. He should know in his period of retirement that he has done a useful job and that the workers, the employers and all of us in this country are grateful to him for his services. He was appointed by the former government, as I am sure the Minister of Labour would agree, in accordance with the requirements of the act, after consultation with the labour organizations of Canada. The issue which is immediately before us is that the replacement which the government has announced is not, it would seem, fully in accordance with the requirements of the act. Certainly it would seem that the new appointment has been made in such a way as not to encourage a measure of cooperation between the government and the representatives of labour.
The points of difference between labour and government are, inevitably, great. Oftentimes the relationship is complicated and no opportunity should be lost to encourage wherever possible the greatest measure of co-operation between the government on the one hand and labour on the other. I am afraid that the government in this instance, whatever may be its defence, has created a situation which in spite of the statement made by the Minister of Labour yesterday will not be regarded as fully satisfactory.

Mr. Chairman, if this particular item that is being discussed at the present time was not of such a serious nature I can assure you that both I and my colleagues would be very much amused with the display we have witnessed for the last while. As the hon. member for Essex East promoted himself or proposed himself as the undying champion of labour, I could not help recalling that at the convention of the Canadian Labour Congress held out in Winnipeg last year I do not recall that the party he represents received any more favourable consideration than did the party that he was castigating at this time. In my opinion, the labour movement of this country, as represented by their Winnipeg convention last year, has written off both parties.
Mr. Chairman, the very point that was expounded so well by the hon. member for Essex East has to do with the fact that the government is now faced with the necessity of increasing the contributions to the unemployment insurance fund. I think he skipped lightly over the basic reasons for this action. If we look back to the time when this unemployment insurance fund was first created I think we will find that it was created for a specific purpose, namely to deal with seasonal unemployment that occurs in this country as a result of climatic conditions. In other words, even if you have full employment in the summer time, owing to climatic conditions during certain seasons of the year certain workers are unemployed. As a result of this situation, this unemployment insurance fund was set up.
This condition has gone on for the past two years and we are no longer faced with
66968-9-214J
Unemployment Insurance Act this problem which the fund was set up to meet. Instead of having seasonal unemployment during the winter months owing to severe weather conditions, we are faced with almost chronic unemployment of roughly half a million workers in this country. The fund which was set up just cannot cope with this. By increasing the contributions of people who are still working we will not cure the cancer in our society which we have today. I think this government must realize that if we are going to condone the fact that we must have chronic unemployment in this country, we had better find a new cure for it, because increasing the unemployment fund to meet seasonal unemployment will not cure the problem with which we are faced today. Certainly you will have to increase contributions if you are going to make the unemployment insurance fund do the job it was intended to do some time ago, because either through the actions of this government or through its lack of action the cost of living is going up in a straight climb, and the contributions which would suffice some time ago just will not suffice today. In addition to that, if we are going to be faced with 500,000 unemployed workers in this country, then you will have to find a new cure for the problem.
Now, Mr. Chairman, there is another point I would like to deal with. This matter has attracted much attention in the newspapers of this country, and I think I am fairly well qualified to speak on this subject. For eight years I was president of a T.L.C. local and for seven years vice-president of the provincial federation of the T.L.C., so I have lived for many years in the domain of the Trades and Labour Congress. We all know that there has been a new appointment to the unemployment insurance commission. I have met this gentleman many times at conventions in the past and I know him very well. I have a lot of respect for him and know the kind of job he has done. He has served for a long period in his capacity as executive officer of the Trades and Labour Congress in Ontario.
I think hon. members must realize, however, that there has been a steady change in the thinking of the labour movement in this country. I also recall other prominent leaders in the old T.L.C. for whom I have great respect. Mr. Chairman, if I may be permitted I would like to name two: Gordon Cushings and Bill Jenoveese. Both these gentlemen were devoted for many years to the trade union movement. Both these gentlemen belonged to the same line of thinking and the same old traditions as Mr. MacArthur. They subscribed to the same line

Unemployment Insurance Act of thought. But here is one difference, Mr. Chairman. Brother Cushing and Brother Jenoveese were trade unionists first and Conservatives second. They fought their battles at conventions and meetings wherever they were held, and in accordance with the democratic traditions of the trade union movement. If they lost their fight then they accepted the majority vote. Brother Mac-Arthur did not follow these traditions, possibly not by his own choice. He was more or less pushed aside by the new thought in the trade union movement.
I recall that at the last convention of the Ontario T.L.C. the subject of political education came up. It was split right down the middle 50-50, and the chairman had to cast the deciding vote. But each year there had been a marked difference in the trend of thought of the members of the trade union movement belonging to the T.L.C. in the province of Ontario. Next year who knows what would have happened. The next year there was a merger and the T.L.C. and the C.L.C. joined together. However, I would still like to pay my respects to Brother MacArthur for the outstanding work he has done in the past.

speechtext: But the fact still remains, whether he agreed or not, the trade union movement did not see fit to carry him along in the new movement which is going on in future. speechtext: The government has appointed Mr. MacArthur to the unemployment insurance commission. If they had appointed him as a government representative, that would be fine as they are entitled to do so, but they have appointed him as the labour representative of this province when in fact he no longer represents labour in this province. So the result is, assessing all the aspects of this question, that this government is trying to ram down a political appointment as a labour representative of this province by appointing him to the unemployment insurance commission.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would be glad to answer the hon. minister if I may. For eight years I belonged to the old T.L.C., the union which would not allow politics to enter the door. The fact is they would not let it in the front door but they had no objections to letting it slither under the back door. I recall the convention in 1955 of the Ontario firefighters in Fort William. I ran for president of the Ontario firefighters and a group headed by the Toronto local caucused against me on this sole question: How can we keep Martin out of the chair, because he is a C.C.F'er? when we have a Conservative government in Queens Park. Now if that is not politics what is? I submit, Mr. Chairman, that politics were every bit as active in the old T.L.C. as they are today in the C.L.C., but instead of bringing them in the front door, they were always slithered under the back door.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. Starr thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. C-43, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext:
The resolution introducing
this bill was before the house on March 4. At that time I gave a review of the substance of the bill. It was sent to the committee on veterans affairs where it was given careful study, and it is again before the house at this time.

It is not my intention to make any lengthy remarks on this occasion but I am prepared to answer any questions on individual clauses.
On clause 1-Paragraph (f) of section 2 of the Veterans Rehabilitation Act repealed.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS REPEALING AND REPLACING ALLOWANCE PROVISIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
I do wish to say briefly
that this bill was of interest to veterans generally and particularly to the representatives of the Canadian Legion who appeared before the committee on veterans affairs. In dealing with this measure, some doubts were expressed and in this connection I wish to quote from page 198 of the minutes of the committee. These were the comments of Mr. Burgess, dominion president of the Canadian Legion:
Having carefully considered the terms of Bill C-31, we believe that none of the proposals contained therein tend in any way to reduce or abolish any benefits which are now or are likely to become available to veterans. The bill appears only to delete those sections of the veterans rehabilitation act which are either no longer applicable or which are provided for in other legislation or regulations.

speechtext:

(Secretary of State):
Department of Transport:
1.	Yes.
2.	Messrs. Robert and Bernard Goineau- for the installation of gasoline pumps and a repair shop for motor boats.

Department of Public Works.
1.	Yes.
2.	Victoria Hosiery Mills Ltd., St. Jean, P.Q., is interested in acquiring this land for plant expansion.
3.	The matter is receiving consideration.
